slides.old_paragraph3: The apparatus accommodated marine mammals without requiring fingers or hands to manipulate a conventional computer input device. The published EVE experiments concern a controller-based interface; their performance measures must be interpreted within that particular arrangement.
slides.new_paragraph3: The sea lion used muzzle contacts to operate the directional buttons while monitoring the separate display. Each input moved the same visible cursor, and the animal coordinated button selection with the cursor's changing position. Reaching a target therefore combined visual monitoring with control of movement through the button array.

slides.old_paragraph3: The authors proposed that reduced tactile access contributed to the difficulty. That explanation was not established by a separate sensory experiment. The observed improvement concerns an interface modification during acquisition, with the animal's behavior and the functioning of the controller evaluated together.
slides.new_paragraph3: The covering was removed after the first few sessions, leaving the individual buttons directly accessible to the animal's muzzle. Button depression then registered a directional input, and the resulting cursor movement supplied visible feedback. The animals progressed rapidly after this change to the contact surface.

slides.old_paragraph3: Walls made some errors ineffective while allowing the appropriate movement to produce a tone. Their role was to support acquisition of directional relationships. Performance in this constrained environment must be distinguished from selecting the correct direction when all movements remain possible.
slides.new_paragraph3: The walls stopped cursor travel along blocked directions, while the open direction led toward the target. Contact with that target produced the success tone and reinforcement. Changing the target arrangement across trials required the animal to use different directional buttons to reach the rewarded location.

slides.old_paragraph3: Later games retained the acquired cursor-driving skill while changing the decision to be made. The training phase thus supplied an input-control foundation. It did not by itself establish that the animal understood the matching rule or planning demands introduced in another game.
slides.new_paragraph3: A common starting position and a changing target location required different combinations of directional inputs across trials. The animal monitored the cursor as it approached the target and changed inputs to adjust its route. Release of a button ended travel in that direction, making the timing of contact part of accurate placement.

slides.old_paragraph3: The feeder therefore changed part of the social context of a session as well as the delivery mechanism. Its introduction did not remove every human influence: staff still managed sessions and the apparatus. The published records distinguish feeder use from the animal's underlying cursor-control performance.
slides.new_paragraph3: Target contact triggered the feeder through the computer's connection to the microcontroller. The valve's pressure change drove the piston forward, delivering fish or ice through the tube. The animal's successful cursor movement thus initiated a sequence linking the recorded game event to the arrival of reinforcement.

slides.old_paragraph3: Session length and willingness to interact are behavioral outcomes that require interpretation alongside the task and reward history. Long participation is different from accurate performance, and neither measure alone captures all aspects of welfare or motivation.
slides.new_paragraph3: Continued participation depended on the animal remaining focused and engaged with the task. Staff ended a session when disengagement or frustration appeared. The prolonged sessions with ice and encouragement retained the same sequence of directional action, target contact and reinforcement, while participation continued across repeated opportunities to respond.

slides.old_paragraph3: Individual differences persisted within the same nominal task. Training history, session availability and early apparatus modifications differed among the sea lions. These records support describing distinct acquisition trajectories rather than assigning one uniform cursor-learning pattern to the species.
slides.new_paragraph3: ANK and SLD reduced their press counts as target-contact latency declined, while REX achieved faster target contact with a comparatively stable press count. The animals therefore changed different components of their performance during acquisition. Press counts and completion times recorded distinct trajectories through the same directional-control task.

slides.old_paragraph3: REX encountered the maze, whereas the other focal animals entered matching tasks. Their advancement conditions therefore differed. Subsequent comparisons in the common cursor task concern their experience of changed consequences, rather than equivalent exposure to one identical advanced problem.
slides.new_paragraph3: Following advancement, all focal animals were offered the familiar cursor task again. Its target-contact requirement retained the directional responses acquired during training. Records from those sessions linked the animals' experience in the maze or matching games to their subsequent movement times and button use in the common cursor task.

slides.old_paragraph3: Targeting was frequent in the recorded behavior, and staircasing remained prominent after advancement. The coded categories describe recurring movements under the experimental rules. They are not direct measurements of the animal's internal representation of the target or its conscious intention.
slides.new_paragraph3: Targeting and staircasing both recurred in gameplay. Targeting used movements toward the target; staircasing alternated directions to form a stepped route. Separate coding connected each pattern of button presses to the path used for target contact.

slides.old_paragraph3: The before-and-after sequence also included continued practice, so failure exposure was not isolated from every other learning experience. The behavioral finding is sustained engagement and improved familiar-task performance following advancement, rather than a randomized demonstration that failure alone produced the improvement.
slides.new_paragraph3: The post-advancement sessions retained the familiar relation between directional button contact and cursor movement. The sea lions continued to engage with that task and reached its targets more rapidly. Shorter periods of button contact accompanied faster completion, linking the recorded improvement to changes in the temporal organization of their responses.

slides.old_paragraph3: The animal sometimes reacted cautiously to unfamiliar objects, complicating interpretation of its very first encounters. Novelty can affect willingness to select an object independently of knowledge about the matching relation. The investigators consequently considered performance over transfer trials as well as immediate responses.
slides.new_paragraph3: The final two novel transfers reached the performance criterion with as few as five errors. Performance across their first 48 trials approached the near-ceiling baseline established with familiar objects. The sea lion applied the matching relation to new object pairs, and successive transfer sessions recorded increasingly efficient acquisition with those materials.

slides.old_paragraph3: The response was still a physical-object selection, so motor control requirements were retained while the memory demand changed. Matching accuracy at a particular delay concerns memory under this trained procedure, rather than a general estimate of every form of sea-lion memory.
slides.new_paragraph3: Removing the sample left the comparison choice dependent on information retained during the delay. The animal still selected the object matching the previously presented sample, and a correct selection produced reinforcement. Increasing the interval extended the time between acquiring that object information and using it to guide the choice.

slides.old_paragraph3: The procedure preserved the same matching requirement while changing its specific materials. Successful transfer therefore linked earlier exemplar training to new choices. It did not require that every novel stimulus be equally attractive or that the animals display identical learning rates across successive tests.
slides.new_paragraph3: The first choice on each novel problem tested use of the identity relation with newly introduced materials. Performance over the following trials recorded how responding developed with additional experience of that problem. Established baseline trials retained the familiar matching preparation, allowing novel-object choices and practiced choices to be evaluated within the same study.

slides.old_paragraph3: The resulting profiles were compared with task latency and button-use measures. This combination linked observations outside a particular cursor trial to behavior within the computerized preparation. The study addressed individual variation, with trait labels remaining operational summaries of rated behavior.
slides.new_paragraph3: The trait clusters summarized recurring combinations of rated behavior, including affability, perceptiveness and diligence. Each animal received scores across several clusters. Relating those scores to latency and button use connected its broader behavioral profile with the timing and input demands of computerized gameplay.

slides.old_paragraph3: The ratings were considered alongside prior task experience and the measured gameplay variables. A profile is not a direct record of how a particular trial was solved. Its relevance comes from associations with the animal's responses, evaluated against the defined task and its conditions.
slides.new_paragraph3: REX received stronger Affable and Cognitive ratings alongside lower Diligent ratings, while SLD combined moderate Affable and Cognitive ratings with higher Withdrawn and Challenging tendencies. These combinations retained several dimensions of each animal's behavior. The profiles described individual patterns across the same set of rated traits.

slides.old_paragraph3: Because the traits were rated rather than experimentally assigned, their associations do not establish that changing a trait would change performance. The findings support considering individual tendencies when interpreting response trajectories and selecting an appropriate level of task challenge.
slides.new_paragraph3: Higher Perceptive ratings accompanied shorter target-contact latencies in both initial and later sessions. The association persisted across the training period, linking that rated behavioral tendency with consistently quicker responding. Dominance ratings were associated with initial latency and initial button use, giving the two trait clusters different relationships with the recorded task measures.

slides.old_paragraph3: The study's associations provide a basis for testing individualized enrichment, but the reported analysis did not experimentally compare alternative personalized programs. A proposed design implication is to adjust difficulty and engagement opportunities while continuing to record the animal's actual response, rather than relying on its trait label alone.
slides.new_paragraph3: The Affable cluster included ratings of cooperation, friendliness toward people, calmness, predictability and confidence. Animals scoring higher on this cluster showed greater reductions in target-contact latency over training. The relationship connected these recurring behavioral tendencies with the amount of improvement across repeated computerized sessions.

slides.old_paragraph3: Consumption was treated as a proxy for participation and health-related interest. The animals' sea pens also contained natural fauna, so offered-diet consumption was not an exhaustive measure of everything ingested. The experimental interpretation depends on that particular managed-feeding context.
slides.new_paragraph3: Daily feeding records identified whether each animal consumed its offered ration, including food delivered during EVE. An incomplete-consumption day marked a feeding opportunity in which part of that ration remained uneaten. Comparing these records across the periods before and after EVE tracked participation in managed feeding over time.

slides.old_paragraph3: The control records help distinguish the focal change from an improvement shared by the entire managed population. The design was a longitudinal husbandry comparison rather than a randomized assignment of enrichment. Its evidence concerns changes associated with introducing EVE within the animals' existing care.
slides.new_paragraph3: The same incomplete-consumption measure was followed across the two periods for both focal and control animals. REX and SLD experienced fewer days with unfinished rations after EVE began, while the controls retained a different pattern. The feeding records therefore preserved each animal's trajectory across repeated daily opportunities to consume its offered diet.

slides.old_paragraph3: Assessing enrichment therefore requires several outcomes: performance under the task's contingencies, voluntary participation, feeding records and health history. The published study combined these observations within managed care. A design that retains those distinctions can evaluate an animal-controlled interface without treating every successful cursor contact as evidence of improved welfare.
slides.new_paragraph3: Feeding records tracked completion of the offered ration and the amount left uneaten, while veterinary records tracked clinically ill days. The game logs separately recorded target-contact latency and button use. Together, these records followed the animals' task performance, feeding participation and health across the periods of managed care.
